title: Nvidia Announces RTX A2000 Workstation GPU
text:
# Nvidia Announces RTX A2000 Workstation GPU

By Jovan 

Posted: November 13,2026 

The smallest ever Ampere GPU isn’t a compact RTX 2060 graphics card, but a brand new card meant to fit into specialized, workstation computers.

This latest piece of tech is another card in Nvidia’s lineup of A-Series GPUs, the successor to the famous Quadro series. The RTX A2000 is the smallest of the bunch, approximately half the size of the RTX 3090, but packing quite a punch in its tiny case. It has 3,328 CUDA cores and 6 GB of GDDR6 memory running at 6,001 MHz. All that combined delivers 8 teraflops of raw computing power, ideal for companies that run rendering farms or research stations that need computer clusters for complex scientific calculations.

This GPU isn’t just compact, but power-efficient, too. Under load, it requires just 70 W of power, while staying cool thanks to the encased design of all Nvidia’s A-Series cards. Of course, the tech giant is working alongside its many partners on delivering a variety of A2000 cards to the market, so expect some wild designs like we’ve seen so far with RTX 2070 GPUs and their younger silicone relatives.

The RTX A2000’s third-generation tensor cores for improved AI, the second generation of ray-tracing features, and PCIe 4 promise better performance of power-hungry apps like 3DS Max and Blender. Its small form factor means there is no need for upgrading to giant-sized computer cases and improved airflow. Nonetheless, it still has enough ports: You can hook up four monitors to it using DisplayPort 1.4 ports, something that is a must as the target audience is used to working at multimonitor setups.

The RTX A2000 launches this October at a recommended retail price of $450. Expect it to appear in premade workstations by Dell, ASUS, HP, and Lenovo, as well as in various flavors made by Nvidia’s partners.

title: NVIDIA RTX PRO 5500 Blackwell appears at $17,999 MSRP, higher than RTX PRO 6000
text:
# NVIDIA RTX PRO 5500 Blackwell appears at $17,999 MSRP, higher than RTX PRO 6000

The RTX PRO 5500 Blackwell has appeared in a US retailer listing for $17,408.63, despite offering less memory than RTX PRO 6000.

Nov 5, 13:30 GMT•WhyCry•2 min read Comments

Set as Preferred Source

RTX Pro Blackwell

© NVIDIA

### RTX PRO 5500 Blackwell 84GB gets first US retailer pricing

NVIDIA’s upcoming RTX PRO 5500 Blackwell has appeared at SHI Government Solutions with a listed MSRP of $17,999** and a discounted price of **$ 17,408.63. The listing covers the PNY Workstation Edition with part number VCNRTXPRO5500B-PB. 

The RTX PRO 5500 Blackwell features 21,760 CUDA cores and 84GB of GDDR7 ECC memory on a 416-bit interface. It offers 1,398 GB/s of memory bandwidth and has a maximum power rating of 600W. This is the same GPU model that Chinese technology companies have reportedly been ordering for AI workloads.

...

The price is somewhat surprising because NVIDIA’s own US Marketplace lists the higher-end RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition at $16,000. That model has 24,064 CUDA cores, 96GB of GDDR7 ECC memory and 1,792 GB/s of bandwidth. We previously reported that NVIDIA increased its RTX PRO 6000 listing from $13,250 to $16,000 in August. Even after that increase, the RTX PRO 6000 is still $1,408 cheaper than SHI’s current RTX PRO 5500 offer.

The RTX PRO 5500 has also attracted large orders from China. According to media reports, ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have ordered more than 3 million cards with a combined value exceeding $35 billion. The reported price is approximately $11,400 per GPU, although this figure concerns large enterprise orders rather than individual retail purchases.

© NVIDIA

Reuters also reported that NVIDIA could not guarantee delivery of the requested quantities. Chinese companies have reportedly ordered more than 6 million RTX PRO 5500 cards in total, exceeding NVIDIA’s planned production capacity. Commercial deliveries are expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027.

We should point out that $17,999 is the MSRP stated by SHI, not an official price announced by NVIDIA. NVIDIA’s own RTX PRO 5500 product page still lists the card as coming soon.

title: Together raised its HGX B200 GPU price and revealed more rates — PricingSaaS Pulse
text:
# Together raised its HGX B200 GPU price and revealed more rates

By Rob Litterst, Co-founder, PricingSaaS

Published Nov 13, 2026

Together raised the price of its on-demand HGX B200 GPU.

Together’s pricing page · Change detected Nov 13, 2026

## What changed

On Together's Dedicated Inference pricing page, the on-demand HGX B200 rate rose from $8.99 to $9.29 per hour, and three GPUs that previously showed "Contact us" now carry posted on-demand rates — HGX H200 at $5.99/hr, HGX B300 at $11.49/hr and GB300 NVL72 at $15.79/hr — per the page Pulse saved on Nov 13, 2026; the Reserved tier still reads "Contact sales" for all of them. On the separate GPU Clusters page, per the same Nov 13, 2026 save, HGX B200 and B300 rates rose across the Preemptible, On-Demand and Reserved tiers, and B300's Reserved rate — previously "Sold Out" — now shows $10.59/hr and $9.89/hr. Together also added a new serverless inference model, Inkling 2 Small, priced at $0.30 per 1M input tokens ($0.03 cached) and $1.00 per 1M output tokens, per Together's pricing page, saved by Pulse on Nov 13, 2026.

## Why it matters

For a product leader buying or reselling GPU capacity, this diff is a signal about Together's pricing posture: the company is comfortable raising rates on hardware it already prices, and it's now willing to post a number for GPUs it used to route to a sales conversation. Posting prices for GPUs that used to read "Contact us" lowers the friction of self-serve evaluation — a buyer can size a workload without a call — but it also removes Together's ability to negotiate case-by-case on those tiers going forward.

...

Not necessarily — Together has now posted public on-demand rates for the GPUs that used to read "Contact us," so it's worth asking your sales contact whether an existing quote beats, matches or loses the new list price before renewing.

# Lambda announces GPU price rises of about 15% — B200, H100 and A100 80GB, from Nov 16

Nov 6, 2026

Read on Lambda's own pricing page today, Nov 6, 2026: the Instances table now prints the prices that take effect on Nov 16, 2026 — HGX B200 up $1.00 an hour, H100 up $0.60 and A100 80GB up $0.40. It is the largest single announced rise we have caught this autumn, and renters have ten days' notice.

Image: GPUJournal price record — read on lambda.ai/pricing

What was announced, in the pricing page's own words (read Nov 6, 2026): 'These prices take effect November 16, 2026, at 00:00 UTC. Until then, log in to your Lambda Cloud account to see current pricing.' The printed Nov 16 rates: HGX B200 $7.69 an hour (from the $6.69 last verified on Nov 5, +14.9%), HGX H100 $4.59 (from $3.99, +15.0%), HGX A100 80GB $3.19 (from $2.79, +14.3%), and HGX A100 40GB unchanged at $1.99. Lambda is also now at a new address — lambda.com — announced on its blog on Nov 5, 2026; the pricing page itself still answers at lambda.ai/pricing.

How we are treating it: an announced rise is not a live price. Our board keeps Lambda's last verified rates until Nov 16 and will move only when the new rates are re-verified in effect on or after that date — the rise is recorded in Price Watch today as announced, with both dates. One consequence of the announcement is already live, though: Lambda's currently-effective rates can no longer be read on its public page, only after logging in, so today's public check could verify the future rates but not re-read the current ones.

What it does to the board when it lands: Lambda's B200 at $6.69 is currently the cheapest verified HGX B200 instance rate we list from a self-serve cloud; at $7.69 it would sit above RunPod Community's $5.98 marketplace rate and just below RunPod Secure's $7.99. Its H100 at $4.59 would remain above the board's best H100 SXM offer (TensorDock, from $2.25 at an 8-GPU minimum) but move Lambda from the middle of the H100 pack toward its top. Around-the-clock, the announced rises add about $730 a month per B200, $438 per H100 and $292 per A100 80GB on a 730-hour month.

title: The RTX PRO 5500 runs the exact same GB202 configuration as the RTX 5090 that launched at $1,999 — the added 52GB of VRAM costs professionals an eyewatering $16,000 markup | TechRadar
text:
The RTX PRO 5500 runs the exact same GB202 configuration as the RTX 5090 that launched at $1,999 — the added 52GB of VRAM costs professionals an eyewatering $16,000 markup | TechRadar

# The RTX PRO 5500 runs the exact same GB202 configuration as the RTX 5090 that launched at $1,999 — the added 52GB of VRAM costs professionals an eyewatering $16,000 markup

 By Rahim Amir 

 Published 12 November 2026 

One launched at $1,999; the other is listed at $17,999

 (Image credit: Nvidia) 

- The RTX PRO 5500 uses the same GB202 configuration as the RTX 5090: 170 SMs and 21,760 CUDA cores
- It is not a complete rebadge, however; it comes with a different board, 84GB of ECC memory, a narrower bus, and pro features
- Leaks and a board partner suggest GB202 is shifting from the 5090 to RTX PRO cards, though Nvidia denies discontinuation

Nvidia insists the GeForce RTX 5090 has not been discontinued, but its GPU keeps turning up elsewhere, with the latest emerging as the RTX PRO 5500, a workstation card that US reseller SHI Government Solutions listed recently at $17,999.

That overlap has fueled claims that Nvidia is simply rebadging its gaming flagship as a pro card to maximize profits while abandoning gamers.

...

As we reported when the card appeared in September 2026, the RTX PRO 5500 packs 84GB of ECC GDDR7 memory using 28 3GB modules split across both sides of the board, compared to 32GB on the 5090. It runs that memory over a narrower, slower interface, so bandwidth falls to 1,398GB/s from the 5090's 1,792GB/s, a 22% cut.

The GPU is rated for 600W rather than 575W, can be split into two isolated 42GB instances, ships with professional drivers, and is built for rack-mounted workstations with blower or liquid cooling. So one could argue that no 5090 is being pulled off a shelf and relabeled. What the two products share here is the silicon, and it's the scarce part at a time when one can't find an RTX 5090 anywhere close to MSRP on shelves.

...

The economics of where those dies go are stark: The RTX 5090 launched at $1,999. In October 2026, Reuters reported that ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent had ordered more than three million RTX PRO 5500s at about $11,400 each, while the SHI listing puts its MSRP at $17,999.

The same GPU configuration is worth roughly 5.7 times its gaming launch price in a Chinese bulk order, and about nine times at that US list price. An extra 52GB of GDDR7 memory is not cheap in the current memory market, but it does not come anywhere close to explaining a gap of that size. Nvidia therefore earns substantially more profit per die in a 5500 than in a 5090, making it a no-brainer to supply the former rather than the latter.

...

Nvidia's response, when it came, was carefully worded. Speaking in Taipei on October 16, SVP Jeff Fisher said that "although the RTX 5090 has other variants, it has definitely not been discontinued." He acknowledged that supply was constrained, but neither he nor Nvidia has said how GB202 output is divided between the 5090 and the other products built on the same chip.

...

Nvidia does not need to rebadge the RTX 5090. The RTX PRO 5500 lets it sell the same GPU configuration at several times the price into a market with more demand than supply, without ever announcing that its gaming flagship is gone. Interestingly, its product page still lists the 5500 as coming soon, with no official price.

# NVIDIA Releases Compact DGX Spark AI Desktop

The Founders Edition packs 128GB of shared memory into a desktop-sized AI system, now priced sharply higher.

Updated on Nov. 12, 2026 in Semiconductors

NVIDIA released its compact DGX Spark Founders Edition AI desktop, packing 128GB of shared memory, and raised its price from €4,399 to near €7,500. AI Illustration. Upload story photo >

NVIDIA has released the DGX Spark Founders Edition, a compact AI desktop roughly 15 by 15 centimeters in size built around the GB10 Grace Blackwell chip with 128GB of shared memory. NVIDIA has also announced a price increase for the Founders Edition, from an original listed price of €4,399 to a range close to €7,500.

...

The system brings substantial AI computing capacity into a desk-sized form factor, giving developers and researchers a local alternative to cloud resources. The steep price increase, however, raises questions about how accessible this class of hardware will be to the individuals and small teams it is designed for.

The GB10 chip, manufactured on TSMC's 3nm process and developed by NVIDIA and MediaTek, pairs 6,144 CUDA cores with 128GB of shared LPDDR5 memory delivering 273GB/s of bandwidth. The CPU and GPU communicate over NVLink-C2C at up to 600GB/s, while the RTX 5070 offers 672GB/s but only 12GB of dedicated GDDR7 memory.

...

The DGX Spark runs DGX OS, based on Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, and includes a 4TB SSD in the Founders Edition. Two Sparks can be linked through the ConnectX-7 interface to combine memory and compute for supported workloads.

## Timeline

1. The Founders Edition was released, with the price increase announced afterward; the extraction does not give exact dates for either event.
2. A review of the DGX Spark Founders Edition was published on November 12, 2026.

...

The DGX Spark extends NVIDIA's DGX line of AI systems into a desktop-scale form factor, moving the company's enterprise-oriented AI hardware closer to individual developers. It positions NVIDIA against rivals seeking to put capable AI computing on local machines rather than relying solely on data-center infrastructure.

Developers and researchers considering local AI hardware now face a price near €7,500 for the Founders Edition, a significant jump from the original €4,399. Buyers should weigh that cost against cloud computing expenses for their specific workloads before committing.

title: GeForce RTX 5070 Ti Hits $1,499: GPU Doubles Its $749 MSRP
text:
Following the near-total disappearance of the GeForce RTX 5090 and GeForce RTX 5080 from mainstream retail shelves, extreme price inflation has officially moved down the Blackwell stack. Launched at an official manufacturer's suggested retail price (MSRP) of $749 in the United States (£729 in the United Kingdom and €884 in Europe), the GeForce RTX 5070 Ti (16GB GDDR7) is now selling for nearly twice its launch price in early November 2026, even as NVIDIA and its board partners insist the graphics card remains in active production.

## Up $160 in Eight Days: From $1,339.99 Baseline to $1,499.99 Custom Models (and Over £1,129 in the UK)

Direct retail price tracking across major North American and European hardware outlets between October 29 and November 6, 2026 reveals a steep upward spike. In the United States, the entry-level price for the cheapest in-stock GeForce RTX 5070 Ti at major retailers including Newegg and B&H Photo Video jumped from $1,179.99 on October 29 to $1,339.99 on November 6. Within just eight days, the baseline street price climbed by $160, placing the most affordable available model 79% above NVIDIA's $749 MSRP.

For factory-overclocked partner cards equipped with triple-fan cooling shrouds, retail tags have officially crossed the 2x MSRP threshold. The ASUS TUF Gaming GeForce RTX 5070 Ti OC (16GB) is currently listed at $1,499.99 at B&H Photo Video, exactly double the baseline launch price. Meanwhile, third-party marketplace listings on Amazon and Newegg have surged as high as $2,770 as baseline inventory dries up.

International markets are experiencing the exact same squeeze. In the United Kingdom, every major PC component retailer now charges over £1,100 for an in-stock GeForce RTX 5070 Ti. At Overclockers UK, the cheapest baseline model sits at £1,129.99 as of November 6, up from £929.99 at the beginning of October and 55% above its £729 official MSRP.

...

## Officially "Not Discontinued" by NVIDIA and ASUS While Only One RTX 5090 Is Given Away

This retail surge stands in sharp contrast to official statements from Santa Clara and its board partners. When End-of-Life (EOL) rumors first circulated regarding 16GB Blackwell SKUs, both NVIDIA and ASUS issued public denials. Both companies explicitly confirmed that the GeForce RTX 5070 Ti has "not been discontinued or designated as end-of-life," stating that all GeForce models continue to ship while attributing shelf fluctuations to industry-wide memory supply constraints.

In practice, keeping a SKU technically active on paper does little to stabilize street pricing when partner allocations shrink to a trickle. The disconnect between official messaging and retail availability was underscored on November 6, 2026, when NVIDIA celebrated the DLSS 5 update for Hogwarts Legacy by launching a social media sweepstakes giving away a single custom GeForce RTX 5090 Founders Edition. Hardware enthusiasts quickly pointed out the irony of proving the flagship GPU still exists by raffling off one promotional unit while retail shelves remain empty.

title: HP launches ZGX Fury desktop with 748GB of memory, priced at $132,000
text:
# HP launches ZGX Fury desktop with 748GB of memory, priced at $132,000

HP starts selling its GB300-powered desktop with 496GB RAM and up to 276GB of combined GPU memory.

Yesterday, 12:21 GMT•WhyCry•2 min read Comments

Set as Preferred Source

NVIDIA Blackwell

## HP ZGX Fury G1n AI Station with NVIDIA GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra

HP has started selling its ZGX Fury G1n AI Station in the United States. The workstation features NVIDIA’s GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra Superchip and comes with 496GB of LPDDR5X system memory. It also includes 252GB of HBM3e GPU memory, bringing the combined coherent memory capacity to 748GB. 

The ZGX Fury is based on NVIDIA’s GB300 platform, which combines a 72-core Arm Neoverse V2 Grace CPU with a Blackwell Ultra GPU. The LPDDR5X-6400 memory provides up to 396 GB/s of bandwidth, while the HBM3e memory delivers 7.1 TB/s. HP claims up to 20 PFLOPS of FP4 AI compute performance.

...

### Up to 276GB of combined GPU memory

HP offers three configurations of the ZGX Fury. The base model relies on the integrated Blackwell Ultra GPU, while the other two add NVIDIA RTX PRO Blackwell graphics cards. The RTX PRO 2000 model includes 16GB of GDDR7 memory for $133,000, while the RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell SFF configuration comes with 24GB for $136,000.

1 / 4

‹›⛶

ZGX Fury AI Desktop © HP

The latter configuration has 276GB of combined GPU memory, although this consists of separate 252GB HBM3e and 24GB GDDR7 pools. The GB300’s 748GB of coherent memory combines the Grace CPU’s LPDDR5X memory with the Blackwell Ultra GPU’s HBM3e memory. HP says the system can support local inference with models containing up to one trillion parameters using FP4 quantization.

### A $132,000 desktop designed for local AI

The workstation uses a liquid-cooled tower chassis that can also fit into a 5U rack. It supports up to 32TB of storage, three PCIe 5.0 expansion slots and two QSFP112 ports offering 400 Gb/s connectivity each. HP ships the system with Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, NVIDIA AI development tools and a 1600W power supply.

© HP

HP ZGX SPECS

The ZGX Fury was announced earlier this year, but its US pricing has only now appeared alongside retail listings. HP is targeting organizations running large AI models locally, rather than conventional desktop users. Despite its tower design, the machine requires a dedicated 200-240V power circuit. At $132,000, even the power outlet needs some planning.
